storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA are fundamentally different in all subjects.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is comparing course lists for B.Com and BBA.
storySpine.observation: Found Business Organization & Management in both Semester I documents.
storySpine.focus: The risk of assuming total degree divergence based on titles.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Evidence contradicts the belief of total separation, requiring further investigation into depth.
storySpine.changedAction: Looking beyond course titles to specific learning outcomes.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Replaces title-based assumptions with a request for specific course syllabus details.
storySpine.channelExperience: The audience learns to verify assumptions using specific, cited evidence.

candidates.title: The Overlap Check
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that degree titles define all subject content.
candidates.viewerChange: Moves from assuming divergence to investigating specific evidence.
candidates.concept: Verification of shared subject titles in official documents.
candidates.device: Split-screen comparison of two official document pages.
candidates.payoff: The viewer stops guessing and starts verifying content using official sources.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management appears in both JOY University B.Com (p.5) and BBA (p.9) documents for 2025-26 cohorts; this does not prove identical depth or assessment.
candidates.support: JOY University PDF: B.Com Accounting & Finance p.5; BBA Entrepreneurship Management p.9.
methodSteps: Identify the specific programme and document cohort.
Show the inspected course-title row in each source.
Use this bounded overlap to investigate the full course.
candidates.interpretationRule: The supplied rows establish this shared title in these documents only.
candidates.visibleProof: Comparison of two official PDF rows confirms identical title presence.
candidates.limitations: No universal overlap, identical content, exclusivity, or career inference.

demonstration.input: Two official course documents showing Semester I subjects.
demonstration.visibleInput: Business Organization & Management found in both.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How does the teaching depth differ for this specific subject?

storySpine.startingBelief: I can decide my degree by looking at a list of subjects.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student identifies a task they want to solve.
storySpine.observation: The task instructions don't explain how it's assessed.
storySpine.focus: Distinguishing task content from assessment criteria.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Knowing the task is insufficient without knowing the evaluation standard.
storySpine.changedAction: Drafts three specific questions for the course team.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Produces a structured inquiry rather than an emotional reaction.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience learns to separate task, criteria, and feedback requirements.

candidates.title: The Assessment Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Confusing task content with assessment criteria.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to formulate precise questions about course requirements.
candidates.concept: Three-column worksheet for evaluating degree-related tasks.
candidates.device: A three-column question sheet: Task, Criterion, Feedback.
candidates.payoff: The viewer gains a repeatable method to evaluate any course task.
candidates.hlni: A task label alone does not specify output, assessment criteria, or feedback; these must be investigated separately.
candidates.support: Logical separation of variables in academic task evaluation.
methodSteps: Write the expected work product.
Ask what criterion is used to assess it.
Ask what feedback is available.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question.
candidates.visibleProof: Completing the columns reveals specific knowledge gaps.
candidates.limitations: This is a question-forming aid, not a degree ranking tool.

demonstration.input: A sample business case study task instruction.
demonstration.visibleInput: Analyze company cash flow for Q3.
demonstration.observation: Grading criteria and feedback mechanism are unknown.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What specific criteria are used to evaluate this analysis?

storySpine.startingBelief: If I can't solve this task, I'm choosing the wrong degree.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student struggles with an illustrative task.
storySpine.observation: The sticking point is a specific detail, not a general inability.
storySpine.focus: Reframing struggle as an investigative step.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Struggle identifies where the student needs more information, not where they lack potential.
storySpine.changedAction: Logs the specific question and seeks clarification.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Replaces self-doubt with a targeted research question.
storySpine.channelExperience: The student feels understood by documenting their process instead of judging their performance.

candidates.title: The Curiosity Journal
candidates.audienceGap: Mistaking task-specific confusion for degree mismatch.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to journal questions instead of judging self-efficacy.
candidates.concept: Recording specific task uncertainties to guide future research.
candidates.device: A physical journal tracking task barriers and follow-up questions.
candidates.payoff: The viewer approaches course research as an investigator, not a victim.
candidates.hlni: A short illustrative activity reveals specific knowledge gaps; it cannot determine long-term academic fit.
candidates.support: Empirical observation of specific task stumbling blocks.
methodSteps: Try or inspect a clearly illustrative task.
Record one point where help was needed.
Turn the observation into a question for a course team.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the observation to choose the next question.
candidates.visibleProof: The journal transitions from frustration to a clear, actionable question.
candidates.limitations: Does not measure aptitude, learning style, or long-term performance.

demonstration.input: A sample task involving resource allocation.
demonstration.observation: Uncertain about how to handle contingency funds.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How are contingency funds managed in this specific module?

storySpine.startingBelief: I must choose between B.Com or BBA immediately.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is anxious about making a final decision.
storySpine.observation: The student has preferences but lacks concrete verification of requirements.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Preferences are not evidence; checking requirements is the next step.
storySpine.changedAction: Creates a checklist of unknowns for their top two choices.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Moves from anxiety to a structured research plan.
storySpine.channelExperience: The viewer feels supported by a clear, non-judgmental next step.

candidates.title: Preference vs. Proof
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming preference equates to program availability/suitability.
candidates.viewerChange: Moves from emotional preference to requirement verification.
candidates.concept: Mapping preferences against confirmed requirement lists.
candidates.device: A checklist of preferences vs. verified facts.
candidates.payoff: The viewer gains clarity by separating what they want from what they have confirmed.
candidates.hlni: An appealing option and an available option are different; unknown requirements should be checked rather than assumed.
candidates.support: Logical separation of desire and factual confirmation.
methodSteps: Name the option you prefer.
List requirements you need to check.
Verify unknowns before proceeding.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use unknown requirements as the next verification task.
candidates.visibleProof: The preference list shrinks as facts are confirmed.
candidates.limitations: Never invent eligibility rules or prerequisites.

demonstration.input: A card listing 'BBA: Focus on Strategy'.
demonstration.visibleInput: Is this programme's strategy module compulsory?
demonstration.nextQuestion: Where can I find the official course requirements list?

storySpine.startingBelief: I can guess which degree an unlabeled task belongs to.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student tries to guess a task's origin based on its description.
storySpine.observation: The task fits multiple programs or none at all.
storySpine.focus: Recognizing the limit of inferential guessing.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: The example is unlabeled; guessing without evidence is unreliable.
storySpine.changedAction: Asks for the source document instead of guessing.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Replaces a false-certainty guess with a precise request for evidence.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience learns that unlabeled tasks don't imply specific degrees.

candidates.title: The Unlabeled Task
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that task style reveals degree ownership.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to identify missing information before drawing conclusions.
candidates.concept: Testing program-specific claims against a neutral, unlabeled task.
candidates.device: A blind test of a business task without labels.
candidates.payoff: The viewer stops making false associations between tasks and degrees.
candidates.hlni: One unlabeled example does not prove degree ownership; an exclusive claim requires information that links the example to the category.
methodSteps: Present one example without a source link.
Separate a guess from what is proven.
Identify the missing source.
candidates.interpretationRule: Answer 'not enough information' if the link is absent.
candidates.visibleProof: The inability to assign the task proves the need for source evidence.
candidates.limitations: Do not assert the task belongs to both or neither without evidence.

demonstration.nextQuestion: Which specific course document contains this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: If the totals are the same, the programs are similar.
storySpine.observation: Different components lead to the same aggregate total.
storySpine.focus: The danger of relying on aggregate totals.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Totals hide the underlying mix of subjects or focus areas.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Shows the viewer why breakdown analysis is necessary.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience experiences a 'eureka' moment about aggregate data.

candidates.title: The Total Trap
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming equal totals imply identical program composition.
candidates.viewerChange: Starts requesting component breakdowns for all comparisons.
candidates.concept: Arithmetic demonstration of how different components produce identical totals.
candidates.device: Visual comparison of two sets of numbers totaling the same.
candidates.payoff: The viewer learns to look at breakdowns rather than superficial totals.
candidates.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot reveal the underlying mix.
methodSteps: Show two component lists with the same total.
Reveal their different components.
Ask for a breakdown.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use the breakdown to see what differs.
candidates.visibleProof: Two columns of different numbers summing to the same total.
candidates.limitations: Illustrative figures only; do not assign to real university credits.

demonstration.input: Two illustrative credit lists (Program A vs B).
demonstration.observation: The subjects making up the 120 are vastly different.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Can I see the list of component subjects for each?

plan.contrast: The selected candidates differ by objective: trust_1 uses external documentation to challenge assumptions, conn_1 provides a personal journaling method to handle uncertainty, and disc_2 uses a visual arithmetic model to teach the need for breakdown analysis rather than aggregate comparison.

issues: Discovery: use a clearly illustrative arithmetic example, not invented programme credits or degree-specific numerical breakdowns.
Connection/Discovery: concepts collide in insight or core storytelling mechanism; renaming props, actors or the CTA is insufficient.
No feasible, distinct candidate combination; revise the alternatives rather than relabel the same tool.
